catalog_quote: The stress mark is ¯, and the unstress ˘. Neither is employed unless the pronunciation of the vowel is exceptionally deep or light. The accent or pitch of the voice is indicated by ´. This is so normally and frequently on the penultimate syllable that the accent is only employed when an exception to the prevailing rule in Bantu transfers the voice-pitch to the first, last, or other syllable than the penultimate. Monosyllables are not accented unless uttered with vehemence.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Johnston's book-wide transcription convention for all Bantu vocabularies in the volume: the 'accent or pitch of the voice' is assumed on the penultimate syllable and left unmarked there; an acute is written only where it falls on the first, last or another syllable. This is NOT a Tsaayi-specific finding: the Tsaayi-tagged list (no. 179 'Nteye, West Teke') is copied from Koelle's 1854 'Ntere' (a Freetown elicitation from one informant), and Johnston conflates stress with pitch in a language family that is tonal (Teke B70 languages are tonal; cf. the Kukuya and Yaa checks). Koelle 1854 (preface p. vi) only says '´ the common sign for the accent' and marks accents word by word (kémo 'one', biéle 'two', bitét 'three'), with no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose voice-pitch is on the first, last or another non-penultimate syllable receive an acute; monosyllables unaccented 'unless uttered with vehemence'. Johnston adds (same page) that high and low tones are shown by ´ and ` and that tonal etymological distinctions are 'not common in Bantu'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level in citation-form wordlists (comparative vocabularies), 1919 convention applying to the whole book, not a phonological analysis of Tsaayi; reported here only because it is the sole first-hand accent remark in any source Glottolog tags [tyi]. It should not be entered as a Tsaayi stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Teke-Tsaayi [tyi] = Guthrie B73a, one of the four West Teke (B73) varieties with Laali B73b (teke1277), Yaa/Iyaa B73c (yaka1274) and Tyee/Kwe B73d; spoken around Zanaga/Bambama (Lékoumou) in Congo-Brazzaville and adjacent Gabon. The only sources Glottolog tags [tyi] that were opened are 19th/early-20th-century comparative wordlists whose assignment to Tsaayi is indirect: Koelle's 1854 'Ntere' (one Freetown informant, Ndsimu of Léséri) was identified with Tsaayi by Guthrie 1964, and Johnston's 1919 list no. 179 'Nteye (West Teke)' is copied from Koelle (his fn. 6). Pacchiarotti et al. 2019 use a 'Tsaayi (Bambama)' doculect [tyi] from Bastin et al. 1999. The earlier scan's 'Loubelo 1987, Description phonologique du kitsaayi' does not exist: Loubelo 1987 is 'Description phonologique du itsaangi, parler de Madouma-Mossendjo' (Université Marien Ngouabi), on Tsaangi B53 [tsa], a B50 language -- a Tsaangi/Tsaayi confusion. The SIL guide 'Téké du sud-ouest' (Raharimanantsoa & Ntsiba Ngolo 2015) is tied by Pacchiarotti et al. to Tyee B73d and may or may not cover Tsaayi.

sources.note: Only a book-wide transcription convention, p. 41 ('In respect to these vocabularies'): accent/pitch marked with acute only when it is NOT on the penultimate, 'the prevailing rule in Bantu' (quoted in statement). The Tsaayi material is list no. 179 'Nteye or West Teke' in Group LL 'The Kwa-Kasai-Upper Ogowe (Teke) languages', p. 553 (PDF p. 571), footnote 6: "Koelle's Ntere or Ba-ntere; perhaps also the speech of the Ba-kamba, Ba-bembe, Ba-kunyi, and Ba-cangi" -- i.e. the Nteye column is Koelle's 1854 data, and no Tsaayi-specific remark on stress is made.

sources.note: All [tyi]-tagged items are overviews, comparative wordlists, dialect surveys or ethnography (listed by Glottolog as an overview/comparative/wordlist/ethnographic/bibliographical); none is a grammar, phonology or sketch. hh.bib has no 'kitsaayi' title anywhere; Loubelo, Fidèle 1987 is 'Description phonologique du itsaangi, parler de Madouma-Mossendjo' (Université Marien Ngouabi, vi+84 pp., listed by Glottolog as a phonology, language code 'Itsaangi = Tsaangi [tsa]') and Loubelo 1990 'Le nom en kitsa:ngi' (Dakar) -- both Tsaangi B53, not Tsaayi.

sources.citation: Koelle, Sigismund W. 1854. Polyglotta Africana, or A Comparative Vocabulary of Nearly Three Hundred Words and Phrases in more than One Hundred Distinct African Languages. London: Church Missionary House. (Glottolog ref 66179; language code tag 'Ntere/Nteke = Tsaayi = Teke-Tsaayi [tyi]', identification from Guthrie 1964).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Preface p. vi lists the signs used: '´ the common sign for the accent, e.g., á, ǎ' -- no rule. The 'Ntere' column (X.A.6; informant Ndsimu of Léséri, 'the only representative of Ntéke' in Sierra Leone, p. 14) carries word-by-word accents, e.g. kémo 'one', biéle 'two', bitét 'three' (vocabulary p. 3). Glottolog's note quotes Welmers 1971: Koelle 'understandably failed to recognize tone, although he marked what he heard as stress'. Not a description of Tsaayi stress.

sources.citation: Raharimanantsoa, Ruth & W. E. Ntsiba Ngolo. 2015. Petit guide d'orthographe et de grammaire du Téké du sud-ouest parlé dans le Pool, la Bouenza et la Lékoumou, en République du Congo (première édition). Brazzaville: SIL Congo.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only modern description of the West Teke (B73) cluster (an orthography-and-grammar guide, pedagogical in form); Lékoumou is Tsaayi territory, so it may cover Tsaayi (Pacchiarotti et al. 2019 tie it to Tyee B73d). Written by a phonologist who has published on Teke-Eboo prosody, so the likeliest place for a tone/accent statement.
